Church would be powerful enough to shield me from the vengeance of the
terrible young man, if I divulged to that establishment. I conceived
the idea that the time when the banns were read and when the clergyman
said, “Ye are now to declare it!” would be the time for me to rise and
propose a private conference in the vestry. I am far from being sure
that I might not have astonished our small congregation by resorting to
this extreme measure, but for its being Christmas Day and no Sunday.

unfortunate little bull in a Spanish arena, I got so smartingly touched

for certain that this bleak place overgrown with nettles was the
churchyard; and that Philip Pirrip, late of this parish, and also
Georgiana wife of the above, were dead and buried; and that Alexander,
Bartholomew, Abraham, Tobias, and Roger, infant children of the
aforesaid, were also dead and buried; and that the dark flat wilderness

with scattered cattle feeding on it, was the marshes; and that the low
leaden line beyond was the river; and that the distant savage lair from
which the wind was rushing was the sea; and that the small bundle of
shivers growing afraid of it all and beginning to cry, was Pip.

Here, in that eerie expanse, the infantile fragments of my identity—tiny Pip, a trembling mite of terror—were etched into the raw fabric of my consciousness, as I beheld the grim procession of headstones and the leaden hush of the marshes stretching beyond.

If I slept at all that night, it was only to imagine myself drifting

calling out to me through a speaking-trumpet, as I passed the
gibbet-station, that I had better come ashore and be hanged there at

inclined, for I knew that at the first faint dawn of morning I must rob
the pantry. There was no doing it in the night, for there was no
getting a light by easy friction then; to have got one I must have
struck it out of flint and steel, and have made a noise like the very
pirate himself rattling his chains.

Each creak of the bedframe, each whisper of the wind, was a summons to the gallows, and I dared not close my eyes, lest the darkness swallow me whole. The pantry robbery, that dire necessity, could not be undertaken in the black of night, for the very act of striking flint would summon forth the devil himself, rattling his chains in mockery of my plight.

the other man was; except that he had not the same face, and had a flat

down, for it made him stumble,—and then he ran into the mist, stumbling
twice as he went, and I lost him.

His attempt to strike me was a feeble flourish, a blow that missed its mark and sent him sprawling into the mist, his stumbling gait a farce of menace. In that fleeting glimpse, I beheld the duality of his nature: a man shaped by suffering, yet defiant in his defiance of the world’s judgment.

had contumaciously refused to go there.

author: dickens

“Trouble?” my sister echoed, her voice a whip crack of inquiry. “Trouble?” Her words, laced with mock sympathy, unspooled into a diatribe of imagined ailments and nocturnal wanderings. The list of my sins—real and imagined—grew longer with each breath, as she wove a tapestry of my supposed transgressions, concluding with her bitter lament: “I have wished you in your grave, and you have refused to go there.”

and every crack in every board calling after me, “Stop thief!” and “Get
up, Mrs. Joe!” In the pantry, which was far more abundantly supplied
than usual, owing to the season, I was very much alarmed by a hare
hanging up by the heels, whom I rather thought I caught, when my back
was half turned, winking. I had no time for verification, no time for
selection, no time for anything, for I had no time to spare. I stole
some bread, some rind of cheese, about half a jar of mincemeat (which I
tied up in my pocket-handkerchief with my last night’s slice), some
brandy from a stone bottle (which I decanted into a glass bottle I had
secretly used for making that intoxicating fluid,
Spanish-liquorice-water, up in my room: diluting the stone bottle from
a jug in the kitchen cupboard), a meat bone with very little on it, and
a beautiful round compact pork pie. I was nearly going away without the
pie, but I was tempted to mount upon a shelf, to look what it was that
was put away so carefully in a covered earthenware dish in a corner,
and I found it was the pie, and I took it in the hope that it was not
intended for early use, and would not be missed for some time.

author: dickens
text: At dusk, I slipped down, each board seeming to shout, “Halt, thief!” My steps echoed with dread until, at the kitchen, I snatched bread, cheese, brandy, a meat bone, and a pastry, all while eluding detection. The pork pie, locked in a jar, I nearly missed, but curiosity led me to claim it as a covert treasure.

author: dickens

I thought he would be more glad if I came upon him with his breakfast,
in that unexpected manner, so I went forward softly and touched him on
the shoulder. He instantly jumped up, and it was not the same man, but
another man!

author: dickens
text: I approached softly, touching his shoulder. He leaped up—a stranger indeed!

“You must taste,” said my sister, addressing the guests with her best
grace—“you must taste, to finish with, such a delightful and delicious

author: dickens
text: “Pray, taste,” Mrs. Joe declared to the guests, her voice crystalline as she presented Uncle Pumblechook’s offering.

author: dickens
text: “He _was_, if ever a child was,” said my sister, most emphatically.

“Hark!” said I, when I had done my stirring, and was taking a final
warm in the chimney corner before being sent up to bed; “was that great

author: dickens
text: “Hark!” I called as I stirred, “is that the great guns, Joe?”

author: dickens
text: “I think you have got the ague,” said I.

author: dickens

author: dickens
text:
All this time, I was getting on towards the river; but however fast I
went, I couldn’t warm my feet, to which the damp cold seemed riveted,
as the iron was riveted to the leg of the man I was running to meet. I
knew my way to the Battery, pretty straight, for I had been down there
on a Sunday with Joe, and Joe, sitting on an old gun, had told me that
when I was ’prentice to him, regularly bound, we would have such Larks
there! However, in the confusion of the mist, I found myself at last
too far to the right, and consequently had to try back along the
river-side, on the bank of loose stones above the mud and the stakes
that staked the tide out. Making my way along here with all despatch, I
had just crossed a ditch which I knew to be very near the Battery, and
had just scrambled up the mound beyond the ditch, when I saw the man
sitting before me. His back was towards me, and he had his arms folded,
and was nodding forward, heavy with sleep.

author: dickens
text: While journeying toward the river, my feet burned, the marsh-cold clinging like iron to my soles. Though I knew the Battery’s path, the mist drove me astray. Swim-passed a ditch, climbed a mound, and there he sat—a figure in drowsy slumber. His back to me, arms crossed, head nodding like a heavy sleeper. Terror seized me; I feared pricked ears.

author: dickens
text:
He held me by the collar and stared at me so, that I began to think his
first idea about cutting my throat had revived.

author: dickens
text: He seized me by the neck, staring with a gaze that could curdle milk.

author: dickens
text:
I was soon at the Battery after that, and there was the right
man,—hugging himself and limping to and fro, as if he had never all
night left off hugging and limping,—waiting for me. He was awfully
cold, to be sure. I half expected to see him drop down before my face
and die of deadly cold. His eyes looked so awfully hungry too, that
when I handed him the file and he laid it down on the grass, it
occurred to me he would have tried to eat it, if he had not seen my
bundle. He did not turn me upside down this time to get at what I had,
but left me right side upwards while I opened the bundle and emptied my
pockets.

author: dickens
text: At the Battery, he waited, hunched and shivering. His breath seemed to chill the air, his eyes hollow with hunger. I offered the file; he cradled it, though his hunger made no plea.

author: dickens

It was not very polite to herself, I thought, to imply that I should be
told lies by her even if I did ask questions. But she never was polite
unless there was company.

author: dickens
text: A woeful prospect—my sister, who never lied, yet now seemed to cloak deceit. Still, her motives, though dubious, were clear: no better use for her tongue than to keep silence when company graced the room.

author: dickens

I pointed to where our village lay, on the flat in-shore among the
alder-trees and pollards, a mile or more from the church.

author: dickens
text: “I refer to our village,” I said, pointing ashore, “midst the alders and pollards, a mile from the church.”

author: dickens

“Yonder,” said I, pointing; “over there, where I found him nodding

author: dickens

But, Uncle Pumblechook, who was omnipotent in that kitchen, wouldn’t
hear the word, wouldn’t hear of the subject, imperiously waved it all
away with his hand, and asked for hot gin and water. My sister, who had
begun to be alarmingly meditative, had to employ herself actively in
getting the gin, the hot water, the sugar, and the lemon-peel, and
mixing them. For the time being at least, I was saved. I still held on
to the leg of the table, but clutched it now with the fervor of
gratitude.

author: dickens
text: Yet Uncle Pumblechook, omnipotent in that kitchen, adamantly refused, waving his hands as if swatting away spectral notions. He demanded gin and water, hot and sweet. My sister, erstwhile stoic, now darted about, mixing, sweating, her once-calm demeanor fraying.

author: dickens

Joe looked at her in a helpless way, then took a helpless bite, and
looked at me again.

author: dickens

author: dickens
text:
And yet this man was dressed in coarse grey, too, and had a great iron
on his leg, and was lame, and hoarse, and cold, and was everything that
the other man was; except that he had not the same face, and had a flat
broad-brimmed low-crowned felt hat on. All this I saw in a moment, for
I had only a moment to see it in: he swore an oath at me, made a hit at
me,—it was a round weak blow that missed me and almost knocked himself
down, for it made him stumble,—and then he ran into the mist, stumbling
twice as he went, and I lost him.

author: dickens
text: Across the fire, a figure in grey and iron awaited—the BRAVO!—limping, hoarse, cold. He gave me a contemptuous glare, swung a wild swing, missed, stumbled, and vanished into the fog.

author: dickens
text:
Mr. Wopsle, the clerk at church, was to dine with us; and Mr. Hubble
the wheelwright and Mrs. Hubble; and Uncle Pumblechook (Joe’s uncle,
but Mrs. Joe appropriated him), who was a well-to-do cornchandler in
the nearest town, and drove his own chaise-cart. The dinner hour was
half-past one. When Joe and I got home, we found the table laid, and
Mrs. Joe dressed, and the dinner dressing, and the front door unlocked
(it never was at any other time) for the company to enter by, and
everything most splendid. And still, not a word of the robbery.

author: dickens
text: The evening’s company included Mr. Wopsle, clubman and parson’s clerk; Mr. and Mrs. Hubble, wheelwright and wife; and Uncle Pumblechook, farmer and carriaged proprietor. Dinner came at half-past one. Upon Joe and me’s homecoming, we found the table set in regal fashion, doors ajar, yet silence reigned. The theft? Unspoken.

author: dickens
text:
I give Pirrip as my father’s family name, on the authority of his
tombstone and my sister,—Mrs. Joe Gargery, who married the blacksmith.
As I never saw my father or my mother, and never saw any likeness of
either of them (for their days were long before the days of
photographs), my first fancies regarding what they were like were
unreasonably derived from their tombstones. The shape of the letters on
my father’s, gave me an odd idea that he was a square, stout, dark man,
with curly black hair. From the character and turn of the inscription,
“_Also Georgiana Wife of the Above_,” I drew a childish conclusion that
my mother was freckled and sickly. To five little stone lozenges, each
about a foot and a half long, which were arranged in a neat row beside
their grave, and were sacred to the memory of five little brothers of
mine,—who gave up trying to get a living, exceedingly early in that
universal struggle,—I am indebted for a belief I religiously
entertained that they had all been born on their backs with their hands
in their trousers-pockets, and had never taken them out in this state
of existence.

author: dickens
text: I bear the name Pirrip, as attested by my father’s gravestone and the testimony of my sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, who wed the blacksmith. Never having beheld my parents, nor any likeness thereof—since their days antedated the invention of photography—I formed my earliest notions of their appearance from the very stones that marked their resting place. The angular letters upon my father’s slab suggested to my youthful imagination a squat, corpulent, sable‑haired man, his locks curling like serpents. From the inscription ‘Also Georgiana Wife of the Above’ I inferred that my mother was flecked with freckles and of a delicate constitution. Moreover, the five modest stone lozenges, each about eighteen inches in length, aligned neatly beside their grave, commemorating five infant brothers who had relinquished the struggle for life almost at its inception, led me to cherish the pious belief that they had entered the world lying upon their backs, their tiny hands forever lodged within the pockets of their breeches, never to be withdrawn during their brief sojourn.

author: dickens
text:
“Hold your noise!” cried a terrible voice, as a man started up from
among the graves at the side of the church porch. “Keep still, you
little devil, or I’ll cut your throat!”

author: dickens
text: ‘Silence, you whelp!’ bellowed a dreadful voice, as a figure sprang from the tombs flank the church porch. ‘Hold your tongue, you imp, lest I slit your gullet!’

author: dickens
text:
A fearful man, all in coarse grey, with a great iron on his leg. A man
with no hat, and with broken shoes, and with an old rag tied round his
head. A man who had been soaked in water, and smothered in mud, and
lamed by stones, and cut by flints, and stung by nettles, and torn by
briars; who limped, and shivered, and glared, and growled; and whose
teeth chattered in his head as he seized me by the chin.

author: dickens
text: He was a frightful apparition, clad in coarse grey, a massive iron shackle biting his leg. Bareheaded, his shoes in tatters, a filthy rag bound about his brow. He had been drenched, mired, bruised by stones, lacerated by flints, stung by nettles, torn by briars; he limped, shuddered, glared, and snarled, his teeth chattering within his skull as he grasped my chin.

author: dickens
text: “Tell us your name!” said the man. “Quick!”

author: dickens
text: ‘Speak your name!’ the man demanded, his tone urgent. ‘Make haste!’

author: dickens
text: “Once more,” said the man, staring at me. “Give it mouth!”

author: dickens
text: ‘Again,’ the man intoned, fixing me with his gaze, ‘utter it aloud!’

author: dickens
text: “Show us where you live,” said the man. “Pint out the place!”

author: dickens
text: ‘Point out your dwelling,’ the man instructed, ‘indicate the spot!’

author: dickens
text:
The man, after looking at me for a moment, turned me upside down, and
emptied my pockets. There was nothing in them but a piece of bread.
When the church came to itself,—for he was so sudden and strong that he
made it go head over heels before me, and I saw the steeple under my
feet,—when the church came to itself, I say, I was seated on a high
tombstone, trembling while he ate the bread ravenously.

author: dickens
text: The stranger, after a moment’s scrutiny, seized me and inverted my form, shaking out my pockets. Within them lay naught but a solitary crust of bread. The church, as if startled by his violent suddenness, seemed to topple head over heels before my eyes, the steeple appearing beneath my feet; when the edifice steadied, I found myself perched upon a lofty tombstone, trembling while the man devoured the bread with ravenous greed.

author: dickens
text:
“You young dog,” said the man, licking his lips, “what fat cheeks you
ha’ got.”

author: dickens
text: ‘You cur,’ the man murmured, moistening his lips, ‘what plump cheeks you possess!’

author: dickens
text:
I believe they were fat, though I was at that time undersized for my
years, and not strong.

author: dickens
text: I deemed them indeed ample, although I was then diminutive for my age and lacking in strength.

author: dickens
text:
“Darn me if I couldn’t eat ’em,” said the man, with a threatening shake
of his head, “and if I han’t half a mind to’t!”

author: dickens
text: ‘Damnation,’ he growled, shaking his head menacingly, ‘I could readily devour them, and truth be told, I am half‑inclined to do so!’

author: dickens
text: “Now lookee here!” said the man. “Where’s your mother?”

author: dickens
text: ‘Now attend,’ the man said, ‘where is your mother?’

author: dickens
text:
“You bring me, to-morrow morning early, that file and them wittles. You
bring the lot to me, at that old Battery over yonder. You do it, and
you never dare to say a word or dare to make a sign concerning your
having seen such a person as me, or any person sumever, and you shall
be let to live. You fail, or you go from my words in any partickler, no
matter how small it is, and your heart and your liver shall be tore
out, roasted, and ate. Now, I ain’t alone, as you may think I am.
There’s a young man hid with me, in comparison with which young man I
am a Angel. That young man hears the words I speak. That young man has
a secret way pecooliar to himself, of getting at a boy, and at his
heart, and at his liver. It is in wain for a boy to attempt to hide
himself from that young man. A boy may lock his door, may be warm in
bed, may tuck himself up, may draw the clothes over his head, may think
himself comfortable and safe, but that young man will softly creep and
creep his way to him and tear him open. I am a keeping that young man
from harming of you at the present moment, with great difficulty. I
find it wery hard to hold that young man off of your inside. Now, what
do you say?”

author: dickens
text: ‘Listen well,’ the man continued, ‘you must bring to me, at the first light of tomorrow, that file and the victuals. Carry the whole lot to the old Battery yonder. Should you obey, and never utter a syllable nor make the slightest gesture betraying that you have beheld me—or any other soul—you shall be spared. But should you falter, or deviate in the slightest particular from my words, I shall have your heart and liver torn forth, roasted, and devoured. Know this: I am not solitary, as you might suppose. A youth lurks beside me, and compared to him I am an angel. That lad hears every word I utter; he possesses a secret, peculiar art whereby he can reach a boy, lay hold of his heart, and seize his liver. No child can conceal himself from him, be the door bolted, the bed warm, the covers drawn over the head, the mind at ease; he will creep silently, insinuate himself, and rend the victim asunder. I, with great exertion, restrain that young man from harming you at this very moment; it is a struggle to keep him from your very entrails. Now, what say you?’

author: dickens
text: “Say Lord strike you dead if you don’t!” said the man.

author: dickens
text: ‘Swear upon the Lord that He strike you dead should you refuse!’ the man commanded.

author: dickens
text:
“Now,” he pursued, “you remember what you’ve undertook, and you
remember that young man, and you get home!”

author: dickens
text: ‘Now,’ he went on, ‘bear in mind the undertaking you have given, recall the youth who lurks with me, and make haste home.’

author: dickens
text:
When he came to the low church wall, he got over it, like a man whose
legs were numbed and stiff, and then turned round to look for me. When
I saw him turning, I set my face towards home, and made the best use of
my legs. But presently I looked over my shoulder, and saw him going on
again towards the river, still hugging himself in both arms, and
picking his way with his sore feet among the great stones dropped into
the marshes here and there, for stepping-places when the rains were
heavy or the tide was in.

author: dickens
text: Upon reaching the low church wall, he hauled himself over it as though his limbs were numb and stiff, then pivoted to seek me. Seeing him turn, I set my face toward home and made the best use of my legs. Yet, glancing over my shoulder, I beheld him still pressing onward toward the river, clasping his arms about himself, picking his uncertain steps among the great stones scattered in the marshes, placed there as stepping‑stones when the rains swelled or the tide rose.

author: dickens
text:
The marshes were just a long black horizontal line then, as I stopped
to look after him; and the river was just another horizontal line, not
nearly so broad nor yet so black; and the sky was just a row of long
angry red lines and dense black lines intermixed. On the edge of the
river I could faintly make out the only two black things in all the
prospect that seemed to be standing upright; one of these was the
beacon by which the sailors steered,—like an unhooped cask upon a
pole,—an ugly thing when you were near it; the other, a gibbet, with
some chains hanging to it which had once held a pirate. The man was
limping on towards this latter, as if he were the pirate come to life,
and come down, and going back to hook himself up again. It gave me a
terrible turn when I thought so; and as I saw the cattle lifting their
heads to gaze after him, I wondered whether they thought so too. I
looked all round for the horrible young man, and could see no signs of
him. But now I was frightened again, and ran home without stopping.

author: dickens
text: The marshes stretched before me as a long, black, horizontal band; the river resembled another such line, less broad and not so sable; the sky was a jumble of long, angry red streaks intertwined with dense black bands. Upon the river’s edge I could just discern the two solitary black objects that stood upright amidst the expanse: one, the beacon whereby sailors steer—an unhooped cask upon a pole, an unsightly sight at close range; the other, a gibbet bearing chains that once had held a pirate. The man limped toward the latter, as if he were that very pirate returned to life, descended, and seeking to re‑hang himself. The thought struck me with horror, and as I watched the cattle lift their heads to follow him, I wondered whether they shared my sentiment. I scanned the horizon for the dreadful youth, but saw no trace of him. Yet my fear renewed, and I fled homeward without pausing.

author: dickens
text:
My sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, was more than twenty years older than I,
and had established a great reputation with herself and the neighbours
because she had brought me up “by hand.” Having at that time to find
out for myself what the expression meant, and knowing her to have a
hard and heavy hand, and to be much in the habit of laying it upon her
husband as well as upon me, I supposed that Joe Gargery and I were both
brought up by hand.

author: dickens
text: My sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, exceeded me in age by more than twenty years, and had earned a considerable reputation among herself and the neighbours for having raised me ‘by hand.’ At that juncture I had to discern the meaning of that phrase for myself, knowing her to possess a hard and heavy hand, prone to laying it upon her husband as well as upon me; consequently I surmised that both Joe Gargery and I had been brought up in that same manual fashion.

author: dickens
text:
She was not a good-looking woman, my sister; and I had a general
impression that she must have made Joe Gargery marry her by hand. Joe
was a fair man, with curls of flaxen hair on each side of his smooth
face, and with eyes of such a very undecided blue that they seemed to
have somehow got mixed with their own whites. He was a mild,
good-natured, sweet-tempered, easy-going, foolish, dear fellow,—a sort
of Hercules in strength, and also in weakness.

author: dickens
text: She was not a woman of comely visage, my sister; and I formed the general impression that she must have compelled Joe Gargery to wed her by dint of force. Joe was a fair‑haired man, his locks of flaxen curling at each side of his smooth countenance, his eyes a vacillating blue that seemed to have mingled with their own whites. He possessed a mild, good‑natured, sweet‑tempered, easy‑going, foolish, dear disposition—a sort of Hercules in strength, and likewise in weakness.

author: dickens
text:
“Has she been gone long, Joe?” I always treated him as a larger species
of child, and as no more than my equal.

author: dickens
text: ‘Has she been absent long, Joe?’ I would ask, ever regarding him as a grown‑child, scarcely more than my peer.

author: dickens

My thoughts strayed from that question as I looked disconsolately at
the fire. For the fugitive out on the marshes with the ironed leg, the
mysterious young man, the file, the food, and the dreadful pledge I was
under to commit a larceny on those sheltering premises, rose before me
in the avenging coals.

author: dickens
text: My thoughts drifted from that query as I gazed disconsolately at the hearth. There, before my mind’s eye, rose the fugitive on the marshes bearing his ironed shackle, the inscrutable young man, the file, the victuals, and the dreadful oath I had sworn to commit larceny upon those sheltering premises, all emblazoned in the vengeful glow of the coals.

author: dickens
text:
On the present occasion, though I was hungry, I dared not eat my slice.
I felt that I must have something in reserve for my dreadful
acquaintance, and his ally the still more dreadful young man. I knew
Mrs. Joe’s housekeeping to be of the strictest kind, and that my
larcenous researches might find nothing available in the safe.
Therefore I resolved to put my hunk of bread and butter down the leg of
my trousers.

author: dickens
text: Upon that very occasion, though hunger gnawed at me, I dared not consume my slice. I felt compelled to keep a morsel in reserve for my dreadful acquaintance, and for his still more dreadful confederate the young man. Aware that Mrs. Joe’s household was governed by the sternest economy, and that my furtive searches might yield nothing within the locked store, I determined to conceal my lump of bread and butter within the leg of my breeches.

author: dickens
text:
“You know, old chap,” said Joe, looking at me, and not at Mrs. Joe,
with his bite still in his cheek, “I Bolted, myself, when I was your
age—frequent—and as a boy I’ve been among a many Bolters; but I never
see your Bolting equal yet, Pip, and it’s a mercy you ain’t Bolted
dead.”

author: dickens
text: ‘You know, old chap,’ Joe remarked, fixing his gaze upon me rather than upon Mrs. Joe, with the remnants of his bite still lodged in his cheek, ‘I myself took to bolting when I was your years—often—and as a lad I fell in with many a bolter; yet I have never witnessed your equal in bolt‑craft, Pip, and ’tis a mercy you have not bolted yourself to death.’

author: dickens
text:
Conscience is a dreadful thing when it accuses man or boy; but when, in
the case of a boy, that secret burden co-operates with another secret
burden down the leg of his trousers, it is (as I can testify) a great
punishment. The guilty knowledge that I was going to rob Mrs. Joe—I
never thought I was going to rob Joe, for I never thought of any of the
housekeeping property as his—united to the necessity of always keeping
one hand on my bread and butter as I sat, or when I was ordered about
the kitchen on any small errand, almost drove me out of my mind. Then,
as the marsh winds made the fire glow and flare, I thought I heard the
voice outside, of the man with the iron on his leg who had sworn me to
secrecy, declaring that he couldn’t and wouldn’t starve until
to-morrow, but must be fed now. At other times, I thought, What if the
young man who was with so much difficulty restrained from imbruing his
hands in me should yield to a constitutional impatience, or should
mistake the time, and should think himself accredited to my heart and
liver to-night, instead of to-morrow! If ever anybody’s hair stood on
end with terror, mine must have done so then. But, perhaps, nobody’s
ever did?

author: dickens
text: Conscience, when it accuses a man or a boy, is a dreadful thing; yet when, in the case of a lad, that secret weight partners with another secret burden concealed within the leg of his breeches, the punishment becomes, as I can attest, most grievous. The guilty knowledge that I intended to purloin from Mrs. Joe—I never imagined myself thieving from Joe, for I never regarded any of the household goods as his—combined with the incessant need to keep one hand upon my bread and butter, whether I sat still or was dispatched upon some trifling kitchen errand, all but unseated my reason. Moreover, when the marsh winds fanned the fire into a fitful blaze, I fancied I heard the voice of the iron‑legged man beyond the door, the very one who had bound me to silence, declaring that he could neither suffer starvation nor defer his sustenance until the morrow, but must be fed forthwith. At other moments I pondered: What if the young man, whose restraint over me had been so arduous, should yield to a sudden constitutional impatience, or misreckon the hour, and presume himself entitled to my heart and liver this very night rather than the next? Should any mortal’s hair ever rise on end from terror, surely mine must have done so then. Yet perhaps no one has ever experienced such a sensation.

author: dickens
text:
It was Christmas Eve, and I had to stir the pudding for next day, with
a copper-stick, from seven to eight by the Dutch clock. I tried it with
the load upon my leg (and that made me think afresh of the man with the
load on _his_ leg), and found the tendency of exercise to bring the
bread and butter out at my ankle, quite unmanageable. Happily I slipped
away, and deposited that part of my conscience in my garret bedroom.

author: dickens
text: It was Christmas Eve, and I was tasked with stirring the pudding for the morrow, using a copper rod, from seven to eight according to the Dutch clock. I attempted the task while bearing the weight upon my leg—a circumstance that recalled anew the man burdened with his own iron—and discovered that the motion of exercise tended to dislodge the concealed bread and butter at my ankle, a predicament most unmanageable. Fortunately I slipped away and deposited that fragment of my troubled conscience within the garret chamber.

author: dickens
text:
“Drat that boy,” interposed my sister, frowning at me over her work,
“what a questioner he is. Ask no questions, and you’ll be told no
lies.”

author: dickens
text: ‘Blast that boy,’ my sister interjected, frowning over her needlework, ‘what an incessant questioner he is. Pose no queries, and you shall hear no falsehoods.’

author: dickens
text:
“Lord bless the boy!” exclaimed my sister, as if she didn’t quite mean
that but rather the contrary. “From the Hulks!”

author: dickens
text: ‘Good heavens, bless the boy!’ my sister exclaimed, though her tone suggested the opposite, ‘straight from the Hulks!’

author: dickens
text:
“That’s the way with this boy!” exclaimed my sister, pointing me out
with her needle and thread, and shaking her head at me. “Answer him one
question, and he’ll ask you a dozen directly. Hulks are prison-ships,
right ’cross th’ meshes.” We always used that name for marshes, in our
country.

author: dickens
text: ‘Such is the nature of this lad!’ my sister cried, gesturing toward me with her needle and thread, shaking her head. ‘Answer him a single query, and he will bombard you with a dozen more. Hulks, as we call them, are prison‑ships lying right across the marshes.’ In our district we invariably applied that name to the fens.

author: dickens
text:
Since that time, which is far enough away now, I have often thought
that few people know what secrecy there is in the young under terror.
No matter how unreasonable the terror, so that it be terror. I was in
mortal terror of the young man who wanted my heart and liver; I was in
mortal terror of my interlocutor with the iron leg; I was in mortal
terror of myself, from whom an awful promise had been extracted; I had
no hope of deliverance through my all-powerful sister, who repulsed me
at every turn; I am afraid to think of what I might have done on
requirement, in the secrecy of my terror.

author: dickens
text: Since that epoch, now sufficiently distant, I have frequently reflected upon how few comprehend the secrecy that dwells within youth when terror grips them, be the fear ever so unreasonable. I was seized by mortal dread of the youth who coveted my heart and liver; I stood in equal terror of my interlocutor bearing the iron leg; I trembled at the thought of myself, from whom a frightful pledge had been wrested; I held no expectation of rescue from my omnipotent sister, who repulsed me at every turn; and I shudder to contemplate what deeds I might have been compelled to perform, shrouded in the secrecy of my terror.

author: dickens
text:
The mist was heavier yet when I got out upon the marshes, so that
instead of my running at everything, everything seemed to run at me.
This was very disagreeable to a guilty mind. The gates and dikes and
banks came bursting at me through the mist, as if they cried as plainly
as could be, “A boy with somebody else’s pork pie! Stop him!” The
cattle came upon me with like suddenness, staring out of their eyes,
and steaming out of their nostrils, “Halloa, young thief!” One black
ox, with a white cravat on,—who even had to my awakened conscience
something of a clerical air,—fixed me so obstinately with his eyes, and
moved his blunt head round in such an accusatory manner as I moved
round, that I blubbered out to him, “I couldn’t help it, sir! It wasn’t
for myself I took it!” Upon which he put down his head, blew a cloud of
smoke out of his nose, and vanished with a kick-up of his hind-legs and
a flourish of his tail.

author: dickens
text: The mist grew denser still as I stepped onto the marshes, so that rather than I charging at objects, the objects seemed to surge toward me—a circumstance most disagreeable to a conscience laden with guilt. The gates, dikes, and banks loomed forth through the fog as if they cried aloud, ‘A boy bearing another’s pork pie! Halt!’ The cattle fell upon me with the same abrupt stare, their eyes fixed, their nostrils exhaling vapour, bellowing, ‘Halloa, young thief!’ A sable ox, adorned with a white cravat, which to my awakened conscience lent a semblance of clerical gravity, locked its gaze upon me obstinately, swinging its blunt head to and fro in an accusatory rhythm matching my own turns, whereupon I blubbered, ‘I could not help it, sir! It was not for myself that I took it!’ Thereupon the beast lowered its head, expelled a cloud of smoke from its nostrils, and vanished with a flurry of hind‑leg kicks and a flourish of its tail.

author: dickens
text:
All this time, I was getting on towards the river; but however fast I
went, I couldn’t warm my feet, to which the damp cold seemed riveted,
as the iron was riveted to the leg of the man I was running to meet. I
knew my way to the Battery, pretty straight, for I had been down there
on a Sunday with Joe, and Joe, sitting on an old gun, had told me that
when I was ’prentice to him, regularly bound, we would have such Larks
there! However, in the confusion of the mist, I found myself at last
too far to the right, and consequently had to try back along the
river-side, on the bank of loose stones above the mud and the stakes
that staked the tide out. Making my way along here with all despatch, I
had just crossed a ditch which I knew to be very near the Battery, and
had just scrambled up the mound beyond the ditch, when I saw the man
sitting before me. His back was towards me, and he had his arms folded,
and was nodding forward, heavy with sleep.

author: dickens
text: All the while I pressed onward toward the river, yet no matter how swiftly I advanced, my feet remained chilled, the damp cold clinging to them as firmly as the iron clung to the stranger’s limb. I knew the route to the Battery tolerably straight, for I had visited it on a Sunday with Joe, who, perched upon an antiquated cannon, had assured me that, once bound as his apprentice, we would share many a lark at that spot. Nevertheless, the mist’s confusion led me to drift too far to the right, compelling me to retrace my steps along the riverbank, upon a shelf of loose stones situated above the mire and the stakes that demarcated the tide. Hurrying with all dispatch, I had just traversed a ditch I recognised as lying near the Battery, and had just scrambled up the rise beyond it, when I beheld the man seated before me, his back turned, his arms folded across his chest, his head nodding forward beneath the weight of slumber.

author: dickens
text:
I thought he would be more glad if I came upon him with his breakfast,
in that unexpected manner, so I went forward softly and touched him on
the shoulder. He instantly jumped up, and it was not the same man, but
another man!

author: dickens
text: I imagined he would welcome my approach with his breakfast, offered so unexpectedly, and thus I advanced with soft footsteps, laying my hand upon his shoulder. He sprang upright in an instant, yet it was not the same individual, but a different man!

author: dickens
text:
And yet this man was dressed in coarse grey, too, and had a great iron
on his leg, and was lame, and hoarse, and cold, and was everything that
the other man was; except that he had not the same face, and had a flat
broad-brimmed low-crowned felt hat on. All this I saw in a moment, for
I had only a moment to see it in: he swore an oath at me, made a hit at
me,—it was a round weak blow that missed me and almost knocked himself
down, for it made him stumble,—and then he ran into the mist, stumbling
twice as he went, and I lost him.

author: dickens
text: Yet this newcomer, too, was attired in coarse grey, bore a great iron upon his leg, was lame, hoarse, and chilled, and mirrored the former in every respect save for his visage and the flat, broad‑brimmed low‑crowned felt hat that crowned his head. All these details impressed themselves upon me in the fleeting instant I had to observe them: he cursed me with an oath, swung at me—a feeble, round blow that missed its mark and nearly toppled him, for it caused him to stumble—then he fled into the mist, stumbling twice as he went, and I lost sight of him.

author: dickens
text:
“It’s the young man!” I thought, feeling my heart shoot as I identified
him. I dare say I should have felt a pain in my liver, too, if I had
known where it was.

author: dickens
text: ‘It is the youth!’ I thought, my heart leaping as I recognised him; I dare say I ought to have felt a pang in my liver as well, had I been aware of its whereabouts.

author: dickens
text:
I was soon at the Battery after that, and there was the right
man,—hugging himself and limping to and fro, as if he had never all
night left off hugging and limping,—waiting for me. He was awfully
cold, to be sure. I half expected to see him drop down before my face
and die of deadly cold. His eyes looked so awfully hungry too, that
when I handed him the file and he laid it down on the grass, it
occurred to me he would have tried to eat it, if he had not seen my
bundle. He did not turn me upside down this time to get at what I had,
but left me right side upwards while I opened the bundle and emptied my
pockets.

author: dickens
text: Soon thereafter I arrived at the Battery, and there stood the true man—clutching himself, limping to and fro as though he had never ceased his nocturnal embrace and shuffle—awaiting my coming. He was perishingly cold; I half‑expected to see him collapse before my visage, succumbing to lethal chill. His eyes burned with a frightful hunger, so that when I placed the file in his hand and he set it upon the grass, it struck him that he might have endeavoured to devour it had he not espied my bundle. This time he did not invert me to seize my possessions; instead he allowed me to remain upright while I unfastened the bundle and turned out my pockets.

author: dickens
text: “What’s in the bottle, boy?” said he.

author: dickens
text: ‘What lies within the flask, lad?’ he inquired.

author: dickens
text:
He was already handing mincemeat down his throat in the most curious
manner,—more like a man who was putting it away somewhere in a violent
hurry, than a man who was eating it,—but he left off to take some of
the liquor. He shivered all the while so violently, that it was quite
as much as he could do to keep the neck of the bottle between his
teeth, without biting it off.

author: dickens
text: He was already thrusting mincemeat down his gullet in a most peculiar fashion—resembling less a man partaking of a meal and more one hurriedly stowing victuals away—yet he paused to sip the liquor. He shuddered incessantly, so violently that maintaining the bottle’s neck between his teeth without biting it off was nearly the utmost he could manage.

author: dickens
text: “I’m much of your opinion, boy,” said he.

author: dickens
text: ‘I am largely of your mind, boy,’ he remarked.

author: dickens
text: “Thankee, my boy. I do.”

author: dickens
text: ‘Thank you, my lad,’ he said, ‘I do.’

author: dickens
text:
I had often watched a large dog of ours eating his food; and I now
noticed a decided similarity between the dog’s way of eating, and the
man’s. The man took strong sharp sudden bites, just like the dog. He
swallowed, or rather snapped up, every mouthful, too soon and too fast;
and he looked sideways here and there while he ate, as if he thought
there was danger in every direction of somebody’s coming to take the
pie away. He was altogether too unsettled in his mind over it, to
appreciate it comfortably I thought, or to have anybody to dine with
him, without making a chop with his jaws at the visitor. In all of
which particulars he was very like the dog.

author: dickens
text: I had frequently observed our large dog at his meals, and now I discerned a marked resemblance between his manner of eating and that of the man. The fellow seized his food with strong, sharp, sudden bites, akin to the canine’s snap. He gulped, or rather seized, each mouthful far too hastily; whilst eating he cast wary glances to left and right, as though danger lurked in every quarter, threatening to snatch the pie from him. His mind was so unsettled over the repast that he could not savour it at ease, nor endure a dining companion without threatening to snap his jaws at the visitor. In all these respects he bore a striking likeness to the dog.

author: dickens
text: “The young man. That you spoke of. That was hid with you.”

author: dickens
text: ‘The youth,’ he said, ‘the one of whom you spoke, the one concealed with you.’

author: dickens
text:
The man stopped eating, and regarded me with the keenest scrutiny and
the greatest surprise.

author: dickens
text: He ceased his feeding and fixed upon me a gaze of the sharpest scrutiny mingled with utter astonishment.

author: dickens
text:
“Why, see now!” said he. “When a man’s alone on these flats, with a
light head and a light stomach, perishing of cold and want, he hears
nothin’ all night, but guns firing, and voices calling. Hears? He sees
the soldiers, with their red coats lighted up by the torches carried
afore, closing in round him. Hears his number called, hears himself
challenged, hears the rattle of the muskets, hears the orders ‘Make
ready! Present! Cover him steady, men!’ and is laid hands on—and
there’s nothin’! Why, if I see one pursuing party last night—coming up
in order, Damn ’em, with their tramp, tramp—I see a hundred. And as to
firing! Why, I see the mist shake with the cannon, arter it was broad
day,—But this man”; he had said all the rest, as if he had forgotten my
being there; “did you notice anything in him?”

author: dickens
text: ‘Well, observe!’ he exclaimed. ‘When a man stands alone upon these flats, his head light, his stomach empty, perishing of cold and want, he hears naught through the night save the roar of guns and the summons of voices. He beholds the soldiers, their scarlet coats illuminated by the torches borne ahead, closing in upon him. He hears his number called, feels himself challenged, listens to the clatter of muskets, catches the orders “Make ready! Present! Cover him steady, men!” and yet is seized—only to find nothing. Why, if I witnessed a single pursuing party last night advancing in orderly ranks—damn them, with their tramp, tramp—I perceived a hundred. And as for the artillery! Why, I saw the mist tremble with the cannon’s roar, even after broad day—but this man,’ he continued, as though he had forgotten my presence, ‘did you discern aught in him?’

author: dickens
text:
“Not here?” exclaimed the man, striking his left cheek mercilessly,
with the flat of his hand.

author: dickens
text: ‘Not here?’ the man cried, striking his left cheek with merciless force using the flat of his palm.

author: dickens
text:
“Where is he?” He crammed what little food was left, into the breast of
his grey jacket. “Show me the way he went. I’ll pull him down, like a
bloodhound. Curse this iron on my sore leg! Give us hold of the file,
boy.”

author: dickens
text: ‘Where is he?’ he demanded, stuffing the remnants of his fare into the breast of his grey jacket. ‘Point me to the path he took; I shall run him down as a bloodhound. Confound this iron upon my sore limb! Lad, surrender the file to me.’

author: dickens
text:
I indicated in what direction the mist had shrouded the other man, and
he looked up at it for an instant. But he was down on the rank wet
grass, filing at his iron like a madman, and not minding me or minding
his own leg, which had an old chafe upon it and was bloody, but which
he handled as roughly as if it had no more feeling in it than the file.
I was very much afraid of him again, now that he had worked himself
into this fierce hurry, and I was likewise very much afraid of keeping
away from home any longer. I told him I must go, but he took no notice,
so I thought the best thing I could do was to slip off. The last I saw
of him, his head was bent over his knee and he was working hard at his
fetter, muttering impatient imprecations at it and at his leg. The last
I heard of him, I stopped in the mist to listen, and the file was still
going.

author: dickens
text: I indicated the direction in which the mist had veiled the other man, and he glanced upward for a moment. Yet there he lay upon the soggy, rank grass, filing at his iron with the frenzy of a madman, heedless of me and of his own limb, which bore an old chafe and was bloody, yet he treated it as insensible as the file itself. My fear of him surged anew, now that he had plunged into this feverish haste, and I equally dreaded prolonging my absence from home. I informed him that I must depart, but he gave no heed; thus I deemed the wisest course to slip away. The final image I retained of him showed his head bowed over his knee, labouring intensely at his fetter, uttering impatient imprecations against it and against his leg. The last sound that reached my ears, as I paused in the mist to listen, was the relentless rasp of the file still at work.

author: dickens
text:
So, we had our slices served out, as if we were two thousand troops on
a forced march instead of a man and boy at home; and we took gulps of
milk and water, with apologetic countenances, from a jug on the
dresser. In the meantime, Mrs. Joe put clean white curtains up, and
tacked a new flowered flounce across the wide chimney to replace the
old one, and uncovered the little state parlour across the passage,
which was never uncovered at any other time, but passed the rest of the
year in a cool haze of silver paper, which even extended to the four
little white crockery poodles on the mantel-shelf, each with a black
nose and a basket of flowers in his mouth, and each the counterpart of
the other. Mrs. Joe was a very clean housekeeper, but had an exquisite
art of making her cleanliness more uncomfortable and unacceptable than
dirt itself. Cleanliness is next to Godliness, and some people do the
same by their religion.

author: dickens
text: Thus our portions were dispensed, as though we were two thousand soldiers on a forced march rather than a solitary man and boy at home; we swallowed gulps of milk and water from a jug upon the dresser, our faces apologetic. Meanwhile, Mrs. Joe hoisted spotless white curtains, affixed a fresh flowered flounce across the broad chimney to supplant the former, and laid bare the modest state parlour beyond the passage—a chamber never unveiled at any other season, which for the remainder of the year lay veiled in a cool haze of silver paper, even draping the four diminutive white crockery poodles upon the mantelpiece, each bearing a sable nose and a basket of blossoms in its jaws, each a mirror of its fellow. Mrs. Joe kept her house with immaculate precision, yet possessed a singular talent for rendering her cleanliness more irksome and intolerable than any grime. As the adage runs, cleanliness stands next to godliness, and certain souls pursue the same virtue through their faith.

author: dickens
text:
Joe and I going to church, therefore, must have been a moving spectacle
for compassionate minds. Yet, what I suffered outside was nothing to
what I underwent within. The terrors that had assailed me whenever Mrs.
Joe had gone near the pantry, or out of the room, were only to be
equalled by the remorse with which my mind dwelt on what my hands had
done. Under the weight of my wicked secret, I pondered whether the
Church would be powerful enough to shield me from the vengeance of the
terrible young man, if I divulged to that establishment. I conceived
the idea that the time when the banns were read and when the clergyman
said, “Ye are now to declare it!” would be the time for me to rise and
propose a private conference in the vestry. I am far from being sure
that I might not have astonished our small congregation by resorting to
this extreme measure, but for its being Christmas Day and no Sunday.

author: dickens
text: Joe and I proceeding to church must, no doubt, have presented a touching sight to compassionate observers; yet the anguish I endured outwardly paled beside the turmoil I harboured within. The dread that seized me whenever Mrs. Joe approached the pantry or stepped from the room was matched only by the remorse that gnawed at my conscience for the deeds my hands had wrought. Beneath the burden of my iniquitous secret, I pondered whether the sanctuary of the Church could avail to shield me from the vengeance of the dreadful youth, should I confide therein. I imagined that the moment when the banns were proclaimed and the clergyman intoned, ‘Ye are now to declare it!’ would be the apt occasion for me to rise and seek a private audience in the vestry. I cannot assert with certainty that I would not have astonished our modest congregation by resorting to such an extreme, were it not for the fact that the day was Christmas, not a Sabbath.

author: dickens
text:
“Mrs. Joe,” said Uncle Pumblechook, a large hard-breathing middle-aged
slow man, with a mouth like a fish, dull staring eyes, and sandy hair
standing upright on his head, so that he looked as if he had just been
all but choked, and had that moment come to, “I have brought you as the
compliments of the season—I have brought you, Mum, a bottle of sherry
wine—and I have brought you, Mum, a bottle of port wine.”

author: dickens
text: ‘Mrs. Joe,’ declared Uncle Pumblechook—a sizable, labor‑breathing, middle‑aged man of sluggish disposition, whose mouth resembled a fish’s gape, whose eyes stared dully, and whose sandy hair stood erect upon his crown, giving him the aspect of one just rescued from choking and now recovered—‘I have brought you the season’s compliments—I bear you, madam, a bottle of sherry, and likewise a bottle of port.’

author: dickens
text:
We dined on these occasions in the kitchen, and adjourned, for the nuts
and oranges and apples to the parlour; which was a change very like
Joe’s change from his working-clothes to his Sunday dress. My sister
was uncommonly lively on the present occasion, and indeed was generally
more gracious in the society of Mrs. Hubble than in other company. I
remember Mrs. Hubble as a little curly sharp-edged person in sky-blue,
who held a conventionally juvenile position, because she had married
Mr. Hubble,—I don’t know at what remote period,—when she was much
younger than he. I remember Mr Hubble as a tough, high-shouldered,
stooping old man, of a sawdusty fragrance, with his legs
extraordinarily wide apart: so that in my short days I always saw some
miles of open country between them when I met him coming up the lane.

author: dickens
text: Upon such occasions we took our repast in the kitchen, thereafter withdrawing to the parlour for nuts, oranges, and apples—a shift akin to Joe’s transmutation from his labour‑garb to his Sunday attire. My sister exhibited uncommon vivacity on this particular day, and indeed she was habitually more affable in the company of Mrs. Hubble than elsewhere. I retain the image of Mrs. Hubble as a petite, curly, sharp‑featured maiden clad in sky‑blue, occupying a conventionally youthful station owing to her marriage to Mr. Hubble—though I know not at what distant epoch—when she was considerably younger than he. Mr. Hubble I recollect as a rugged, broad‑shouldered, stooping elder, redolent of sawdust, whose legs lay extraordinarily asunder, so that in my youthful peregrinations I would often discern miles of open field stretching between us whenever I encountered him ascending the lane.

author: dickens
text:
“Especially,” said Mr. Pumblechook, “be grateful, boy, to them which
brought you up by hand.”

author: dickens
text: ‘Above all,’ Mr. Pumblechook urged, ‘be thankful, lad, to those who raised you by hand.’

author: dickens
text:
What an excellent example of the power of dress, young Oliver Twist
was! Wrapped in the blanket which had hitherto formed his only
covering, he might have been the child of a nobleman or a beggar; it
would have been hard for the haughtiest stranger to have assigned him
his proper station in society. But now that he was enveloped in the old
calico robes which had grown yellow in the same service, he was badged
and ticketed, and fell into his place at once—a parish child—the orphan
of a workhouse—the humble, half-starved drudge—to be cuffed and
buffeted through the world—despised by all, and pitied by none.

author: dickens
text: Behold a striking testament to the tyranny of tailor’s work, this young Oliver Twist! Swathed in the solitary blanket that had hitherto constituted his entire wardrobe, he might have passed for the scion of a duke or the offspring of a mendicant; the proudest aristocrat would have stumbled in assigning the infant his proper niche in the great hierarchy of mankind. But once invested in the antiquated calico vestments, yellowed by generations of parish service, he was branded and catalogued, sinking instantly into his ordained groove—a parish foundling, the workhouse orphan, the lowly, half-famished drudge—destined to be knocked about and battered through the world’s thoroughfares, scorned by the multitude, unwept by any.

author: dickens
text:
The members of this board were very sage, deep, philosophical men; and
when they came to turn their attention to the workhouse, they found out
at once, what ordinary folks would never have discovered—the poor
people liked it! It was a regular place of public entertainment for the
poorer classes; a tavern where there was nothing to pay; a public
breakfast, dinner, tea, and supper all the year round; a brick and
mortar elysium, where it was all play and no work. “Oho!” said the
board, looking very knowing; “we are the fellows to set this to rights;
we’ll stop it all, in no time.” So, they established the rule, that all
poor people should have the alternative (for they would compel nobody,
not they), of being starved by a gradual process in the house, or by a
quick one out of it. With this view, they contracted with the
water-works to lay on an unlimited supply of water; and with a
corn-factory to supply periodically small quantities of oatmeal; and
issued three meals of thin gruel a day, with an onion twice a week, and
half a roll of Sundays. They made a great many other wise and humane
regulations, having reference to the ladies, which it is not necessary
to repeat; kindly undertook to divorce poor married people, in
consequence of the great expense of a suit in Doctors’ Commons; and,
instead of compelling a man to support his family, as they had
theretofore done, took his family away from him, and made him a
bachelor! There is no saying how many applicants for relief, under
these last two heads, might have started up in all classes of society,
if it had not been coupled with the workhouse; but the board were
long-headed men, and had provided for this difficulty. The relief was
inseparable from the workhouse and the gruel; and that frightened
people.

author: dickens
text: The guardians of this establishment were profoundly sage, abysmally deep, and eminently philosophical gentlemen; and when they deigned to direct their intellects toward the workhouse, they instantly penetrated a mystery that would have baffled common understandings—the paupers actually *enjoyed* their residence! It served as a perpetual palace of diversion for the indigent; a tavern demanding no reckoning; a ceaseless round of breakfast, dinner, tea, and supper throughout the twelvemonth; a brick-and-mortar Elysium where labour was unknown and leisure absolute. “Ha!” cried the Board, with an air of profound penetration; “we are the very fellows to remedy this abuse; we shall put a stop to it forthwith.” Accordingly, they decreed that the destitute should possess the alternative—for they would compel no man, oh no—of perishing by inches within the walls, or by a swifter method without. With this benevolent aim, they negotiated with the water-works for an unbounded torrent; and with a corn-factor for periodic pittances of oatmeal; and ordained three daily meals of watery gruel, an onion bi-weekly, and half a roll on Sundays. They enacted a multitude of other wise and tender ordinances concerning the female sex, which decorum forbids rehearsing; they charitably undertook to sunder married couples, sparing them the ruinous expense of a suit in Doctors’ Commons; and, instead of enforcing a husband’s duty to maintain his family, as heretofore, they relieved him of his encumbrances and restored him to the blessings of celibacy! One shudders to think what crowds of claimants these two latter clauses might have summoned from every stratum of society, had they not been yoked to the workhouse and the gruel; but the Board were far-sighted men, and had forestalled the difficulty. Relief was made inseparable from the House and the porridge; and that prospect frightened the applicants away.

author: dickens
text:
Let it not be supposed by the enemies of “the system,” that, during the
period of his solitary incarceration, Oliver was denied the benefit of
exercise, the pleasure of society, or the advantages of religious
consolation. As for exercise, it was nice cold weather, and he was
allowed to perform his ablutions every morning under the pump, in a
stone yard, in the presence of Mr. Bumble, who prevented his catching
cold, and caused a tingling sensation to pervade his frame, by repeated
applications of the cane. As for society, he was carried every other
day into the hall where the boys dined, and there sociably flogged as a
public warning and example. And so far from being denied the advantages
of religious consolation, he was kicked into the same apartment every
evening at prayer-time, and there permitted to listen to, and console
his mind with, a general supplication of the boys, containing a special
clause, therein inserted by authority of the board, in which they
entreated to be made good, virtuous, contented, and obedient, and to be
guarded from the sins and vices of Oliver Twist: whom the supplication
distinctly set forth to be under the exclusive patronage and protection
of the powers of wickedness, and an article direct from the manufactory
of the very Devil himself.

author: dickens
text: Let not the adversaries of “the system” imagine that, during the term of his solitary confinement, Oliver was deprived of the salutary benefits of exercise, the solace of society, or the comforts of spiritual consolation. Regarding exercise: the weather being sharp and frosty, he was permitted to perform his morning ablutions beneath the pump in a stone courtyard, under the superintendence of Mr. Bumble, who prevented a chill from settling on his frame by the frequent application of the cane, causing a most salutary tingling to diffuse itself through his extremities. Regarding society: he was conveyed every alternate day into the dining-hall where the boys assembled, and there sociably flagellated as a public spectacle and warning. And far from being denied religious privilege, he was kicked into the same apartment each evening at prayer-time, there to listen to, and derive comfort from, a general supplication of the boys, into which a special clause had been inserted by Board authority, wherein they petitioned to be rendered good, virtuous, contented, and obedient, and to be shielded from the sins and vices of Oliver Twist—whom the prayer explicitly designated as being under the exclusive patronage of the Powers of Darkness, and a direct manufacture of the Devil himself.

author: dickens
text:
Mr. Gamfield gave an arch look at the faces round the table, and,
observing a smile on all of them, gradually broke into a smile himself.
The bargain was made. Mr. Bumble, was at once instructed that Oliver
Twist and his indentures were to be conveyed before the magistrate, for
signature and approval, that very afternoon.

author: dickens
text: Mr. Gamfield cast a sly, knowing glance at the visages encircling the table, and, detecting a grin upon every countenance, gradually expanded his own features into a smile. The compact was sealed. Mr. Bumble received immediate instructions that Oliver Twist and his indentures were to be presented before the magistrate for signature and ratification that very afternoon.

author: dickens
text:

hungry and destitute situation of the infant orphan was duly reported

situation to impart to Oliver Twist, the consolation and nourishment of

magnanimously and humanely resolved, that Oliver should be “farmed,”

inconvenience of too much food or too much clothing, under the parental
superintendence of an elderly female, who received the culprits at and
for the consideration of sevenpence-halfpenny per small head per week.

a great deal may be got for sevenpence-halfpenny, quite enough to
overload its stomach, and make it uncomfortable. The elderly female was
a woman of wisdom and experience; she knew what was good for children;

use, and consigned the rising parochial generation to even a shorter
allowance than was originally provided for them. Thereby finding in the
lowest depth a deeper still; and proving herself a very great
experimental philosopher.
